title: Fructose, Advanced Glycation, and Metabolic Dysfunction: Molecular Pathways Linking Oxidative Stress, Inflammation, and Masld
content: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is a major metabolic disorder associated with obesity, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, and increased cardiovascular risk. Excessive fructose consumption has been implicated in hepatic lipid accumulation, advanced glycation end product (AGE) formation, oxidative stress, and chronic inflammation, potentially contributing to interconnected hepatic and cardiovascular disturbances. This narrative review examines the metabolic and molecular pathways linking fructose metabolism, AGE–RAGE signaling, and cardiometabolic dysfunction, with particular emphasis on the liver–heart axis. Fructose metabolism increases the availability of lipogenic substrates and reactive carbonyl intermediates, which may promote hepatic de novo lipogenesis and endogenous AGE formation. AGE–RAGE signaling can activate oxidative and inflammatory pathways, including reactive oxygen species production, NF-κB signaling, and mitochondrial dysfunction, potentially contributing to hepatic injury, insulin resistance, endothelial dysfunction, and adverse cardiovascular remodeling. Experimental studies provide mechanistic evidence linking fructose exposure and AGE–RAGE-related pathways to hepatic and cardiovascular injury. However, human studies primarily provide separate evidence concerning fructose intake, hepatic steatosis, AGE levels, and cardiovascular risk markers, rather than establishing AGE–RAGE signaling as a mediator connecting fructose exposure to liver and cardiovascular outcomes. Therefore, a major unresolved question is whether AGE–RAGE signaling represents a clinically relevant mechanistic link between fructose-associated liver dysfunction and cardiovascular complications in humans, or whether these processes reflect partially independent metabolic and inflammatory pathways. By integrating experimental and clinical evidence, this review identifies potential therapeutic targets and research priorities while highlighting the need for longitudinal and mechanistic human studies to clarify the clinical relevance of the liver–heart axis.
